newsitem.title: UK: Western Europe redefines role of gasoline exporter.
newsitem.headline: Western Europe redefines role of gasoline exporter.

text.p: Western Europe is redefining its role as a traditional gasoline exporter as it loses market share in the U.S. and feeds a growing appetite from Eastern Europe and Africa, industry analysts said.
And exports to the U.S. may be limited if any life is breathed into European gasoline demand, which has been static for the last few years as popularity grew for diesel cars.
"I think it's fairly likely that Europe will export more to Africa but it's fairly small amounts and the only market of any size is South Africa," said Colin Birch, consultant at Purvin and Gertz.
"The gasoline growth in Eastern Europe is more likely to soak up exports," he said.
"The European refiners had to push their product into markets and now there is a pull for their product," said Keith Hamm, chairman of Petroleum Economics Ltd.
Trans-Atlantic exports fell sharply in 1995 as European refiners adjusted to U.S. requirements for cleaner-burning fuels such as reformulated gasoline.
But some of that drop was replaced by imports of gasoline blending components, which more than doubled from 1994 to 1995, according to data released by the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

"In general the U.S. is importing a lot more out of Latin America and domestically producing more, so they are importing less from Europe," said Peter Bogin, associate director at Cambridge Energy Research Associates in Paris.
Exports to the U.S. were expected to pick up this year and then stabilise or move slightly higher next year, which means its share of the growing U.S. market will be whittled away.
Western Europe, led by the U.K., Spain, Netherlands, Italy and France, captured 33 percent of the U.S. gasoline import pie in 1994 with 42.7 million barrels, the EIA said.
That share dropped to 20 percent or 19.4 million barrels in 1995.

Europe held the same share of U.S. imports in the first eight months of this year versus a year ago, at 22-23 percent, the EIA said, but total volumes rose to 21.8 million barrels from 14.7 million in the year ago period.
Europe has a net export potential of 500,000 bpd and supplies to the U.S. could rebound to 200,000 bpd this year and to 200,000-300,000 bpd in 1997, Hamm said.

In Poland, demand is stretching by 4-5 percent annually and its current consumption of 4.5 million tonnes is satisfied by 1.5 million tonnes, or 12.6 million barrels, of imports, according to a trader at a European refinery.
Most imports come from western Europe because it is easier and cheaper to ship by sea than rail, and because gasoline from nearby Russia has higher taxes, he said.

"It is not more volume than is sold to the States but I think it has increased because the Eastern European markets are growing and existing refinery capacity in the region does not meet the market demands," he said.
European gasoline exports to non-OECD European countries edged up from 1.9 million tonnes in 1993 to 2.3 million in 1994 and 2.2 million last year, the IEA said.
European gasoline exports to Africa were about 1.55 million tonnes in 1995 and in the first half of this year were 1.05 million tonnes, Birch said.

South Africa's demand for gasoline is expected to reach 196,000 barrels per day this year, close to its output of 211,000 bpd. Annual growth of 8.7 percent is expected to turn it into a net importer in the next year -- with Asia supplying some of its needs -- after years of self-sufficiency.
